assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed how trade is modelled. It showed that gains from trade operate through reallocation across firms and not only across sectors. It reshaped theory, firm-level data work and policy analysis in the decades after Krugman's prize. The empirical programme with micro data is large and durable.
assessment.attribution: The Melitz (2003) selection model is the clearest anchor. Helpman's work, including with Melitz and Yeaple on exports versus FDI, is the other core strand. Other key contributors, such as Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, are not in this credited set. Redding is credited but is more a later extender, so I leave him out.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 2003 onward, with more than two decades of replication, extension and use in quantitative evaluation. It is mature enough for recognition.
uncertainties: The credited set omits some co-originators of the firm-level trade literature, so the three-person limit may be contested.
Quantitative trade models may be judged by the Committee to be a competing and partly overlapping basis for recognition.
My assessment relies on general knowledge, not independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's credit-cycle model shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a foundational mechanism in modern macro-finance and financial-crisis analysis. It has shaped central-bank and academic thinking about balance-sheet channels, and it matters more after 2008.
assessment.attribution: The Kiyotaki–Moore (1997) paper is the clear core and a compact, identifiable pair. Gertler and Gilchrist are important in the financial-accelerator and empirical strand, which overlaps with Bernanke's already-recognised work. I restrict credit to the originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism.
assessment.maturity: The model is nearly three decades old and thoroughly absorbed into teaching, DSGE models with financial frictions and policy practice. Its impact has been tested in the Great Recession and later episodes.
uncertainties: The Committee may regard the 2022 prize for banking and financial crises as already covering part of this territory.
Whether to include Gertler, with the accelerator literature, is an open attribution question.
Empirical quantification of the mechanism is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework turned income-gap accounting into a measurable question about the distortion of resources across firms. It links micro data to aggregate productivity differences across countries. It also gave growth and development economics a shared, widely used measurement method.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh–Klenow (2009) is the central, widely used framework. Restuccia–Rogerson (2008) is a closely parallel contribution. Rogerson is not in the credited set, so I keep the proposal to the two authors of the measurement framework. Restuccia's credit is real, but the set is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: The work is over fifteen years old, with a large follow-on literature and policy use. Measurement and interpretation debates continue.
uncertainties: Measurement-error and markup-interpretation critiques bear on how much of the dispersion is true misallocation.
The credited set omits a major parallel originator, which complicates the three-person attribution.
The overall 'income differences' question was partly addressed by earlier growth prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law-and-finance research showed that investor protection and legal institutions are systematically related to financial development and ownership structure. It opened a large empirical comparative-institutions literature that influenced corporate governance, development and political economy. Its reach across fields is very broad.
assessment.attribution: The core 1990s LLSV papers are the identifiable anchor, and the limit of three laureates points to La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes and Shleifer. Vishny is a major co-author of the corporate-governance strand, but I leave him out of the proposed three.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly thirty years old, with extensive follow-up, replication and criticism. Its impact is established.
uncertainties: The legal-origins hypothesis has been challenged on measurement, causality and the persistence of origin effects.
Reputational controversy around one credited person may affect the Committee's view.
The contribution may be judged an influential research programme rather than a settled discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: They assembled a long-run dataset of financial crises, sovereign defaults and inflation across eight centuries. The data revealed recurring patterns and reshaped how crises are studied and anticipated. I find this kind of archival measurement compelling, because it creates evidence that changes what economists know and how they know it.
assessment.attribution: The credit is clearly shared as a pair, through 'This Time Is Different' and related papers. The dataset and the historical framing are their joint achievement.
assessment.maturity: The central book is from 2009, and the data and arguments have been used widely since. Policy influence is large and confirmed.
uncertainties: The 2010 growth-and-debt paper was criticised for data handling and weak causal interpretation. The Committee may weigh this heavily even though it is separate from the crisis-history dataset.
Whether the work is primarily empirical synthesis or an identifiable new method or insight is debatable.
Rogoff's other work, such as in B046, may be considered separately.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The China-shock research gave credible, geographically detailed evidence that import competition can cause long-lasting local labour-market harm. It changed trade and labour policy debate. The task-based labour-demand framework is also influential, in explaining technology and job polarisation.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock papers were written by the trio of Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Autor's task-approach work involved co-authors who are not credited here (notably Levy and Murnane). Katz's links belong to a different strand and to earlier prizes. I propose the empirical trade-shock trio.
assessment.maturity: The 2013 core paper is relatively recent but has clear impact and many replications. Long-run adjustment results continue to accumulate.
uncertainties: The recent 2023 and 2024 prizes covered labour-market and technology-institution themes, which may affect timing.
Some results have been debated or qualified in later work on persistence and magnitudes.
The task-approach strand is attributed to people outside this credited set.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The long-run top-income series built from tax records reopened the measurement of inequality and made distributional national accounts a mainstream topic. This is a substantial data-building contribution of the kind I value, and it has a very large scholarly and public impact.
assessment.attribution: The Piketty–Saez top-income series is the core. Zucman's work on offshore wealth and distributional accounts is important and builds on this agenda, but it is newer. Saez also appears in B014, so his credit is shared across candidates.
assessment.maturity: The foundational series dates from the early 2000s, and the broader agenda is well established. Its use in policy is broad, but work on wealth measurement is still developing.
uncertainties: Measurement choices about capital income, taxes and transfers are contested, and some findings are disputed.
Public and political prominence could affect the Committee's reception.
Assessing the theory content of the wealth-inequality arguments, as against the data contribution, is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Present-bias and reference-dependent models gave behavioural economics tractable formal foundations. They are used in savings, health, consumption and contract design. Rabin's work on psychology and economics and Laibson's quasi-hyperbolic discounting are the best-known pillars.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread over many people, including O'Donoghue, Koszegi and Loewenstein. The three-person limit makes it a difficult attribution. I propose Laibson and Rabin as the most recognisable architects of the formal models, with some risk of overlooking others.
assessment.maturity: The foundations date from the 1990s and 2000s and are now well established. The field was recognised through the 2017 prize, and the new increment would have to be argued on formalisation rather than on the founding insight.
uncertainties: The 2017 prize for behavioural economics may reduce the Committee's appetite for another award in the area.
Replicability and the field's mixed external validity are debated for some behavioural phenomena.
Attribution across five credited names is hard to settle.
